sport!

. . .

<br /> <br />

> Our role is to...Provide for the exchange of ideas and information between

sport]{.cyan} today, and perhaps entice you to work in this space in future!

## Rapid growth into "awkward adolescence" {.smaller}

Technology changes:

- Video
- Wearable and portable technologies
- Count statistics to detailed event data (play-by-play)
- High-speed video
- Multi-camera OTS

Analytical practices:

- Notational analysis
- Programmatic approaches to working with data
- Accessibility of statistical modelling outside of academia
- Computer vision
- Integrating data from multiple sources (across disciplines)

Dedicated tertiary courses for sports analytics

Growth in private sports data and technology providers, advancements in volume and accessibility of data supplied by governing bodies and broadcast partners

Competitor behaviours

## From counts to sequences

[Early days:]{.cyan} Deriving performance indicators from counts of game actions

@sampaio2006: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/17461390600676200

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Research question"}
Can player statistics be used to discriminate between playing positions in basketball?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Data"}
Box score statistics from three professional men's basketball leagues, 2000-2001 playoffs:

- NBA (USA): 5 games
- ACB (Spain): 3 games
- LCB (Portugal): 4 games
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Analysis"}
Discriminant analysis - structure coefficients greater than |0.30| identified as being powerful contributors to each discriminant function.

Cross-validation via leave-one-out method
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Selected results"}
NBA, as an example

Discriminant analysis:

- Function 1 (77% of variance between players, sig.): Assists (neg), off rebounds, 3 pointers missed (discriminating centres from forwards and guards)
- Function 2 (23% of variance between players, sig.): Assists, def rebounds (neg), 2 pointers made, free throws made, free throws missed (discriminating guards from forwards)

Cross-validation:

- 98% of guards correctly predicted (n = 43)
- 75% of forwards correctly predicted (n = 28); 25% incorrectly predicted as guards
- 71% of centres correctly predicted (n = 17); 29% incorrectly predicted as forwards
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="Observations"}
Small data set

Some insight into overlapping roles and skills across positional groups

Largely confirms patterns observable from simple summaries of raw count data and visual observation --  centres notably contribute via greater rebounding and fewer assists (as compared to forwards and guards), guards notably contribute via greater assists, scoring, and scoring attempts (as compared to forwards).
:::

## Continuing to mature as a profession {.smaller}

[Challenges?]{.yellow}

Growth in sports analytics has been rapid but uneven

- Some sports / orgs have been faster to adapt / implement
- Resourcing differences between sports and organisations within sports

Sometimes growing in ways we're not quite ready for ("running before walking")

- E.g., focus on hiring data scientists / analytics specialists without
  understanding and investing in infrastructure and support functions upstream
  (IT, data engineering, data governance)
- Varying maturity in leaders' skills in using and interpreting data to inform
  their decisions

Role clarity and integration within a performance team

- Looking for the mix of domain, interpersonal, data and analytics, and computer
  science / programming skills
- Is analytics a distinct role? Is it better to upskill an SME? Is it just sport
  science with larger data sets?

[Opportunities?]{.yellow}

Many rich sources of data across disciplines, although the industry generally
lacks sufficient mathematical / statistical knowledge to analyse in
sophisticated and robust ways ("we don't know what we don't know") --
opportunities for those with specialist skill sets to make an impact
